query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under service loading conditions, even a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single‐phase solid solution loses toughness due to the diffusion and segregation of trace interstitial impurities (e.g., oxygen and nitrogen) that induce nanoscale precipitate (or intermetallic) formation at grain boundaries and within the matrix. These precipitates serve as stress concentrators that promote brittle crack initiation and propagation under high mechanical load.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase solid solution high-entropy alloy (e.g., a Ti–V–Nb–Ta RHEA) with trace interstitial impurities uniformly distributed.
generation.intervention: Subjecting samples to controlled thermal aging (or service‐like thermal/mechanical cycling) in environments that encourage interstitial diffusion versus an inert (oxygen/nitrogen controlled) environment.
generation.conditions: Service‐relevant temperatures (e.g., 700–800°C) and cyclic or static high-load mechanical testing, where oxygen/nitrogen exposures are either allowed (typical ambient processing conditions) or minimized.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale precipitates or secondary brittle intermetallic phases along grain boundaries and within the matrix due to interstitial segregation.
generation.mechanism: In service at elevated temperatures and under mechanical loading, trace oxygen/nitrogen (initially beneficial for solid solution strengthening) diffuse and segregate. This segregation lowers the energy barrier for the nucleation of brittle second phases. The emerging precipitates interrupt homogeneous deformation and become preferential sites for crack initiation, thus reducing overall toughness and leading to brittle fracture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples aged/exposed to oxygen/nitrogen rich conditions will show the appearance of nanoscale precipitates, a loss of ductility and fracture toughness (exhibiting cleavage facets and reduced work-to-fracture), while those processed under minimal impurity conditions will largely retain their original toughness.
generation.baseline: Initial single-phase, homogeneous microstructure with high toughness and ductility measured prior to aging or service loading.
generation.boundary: Applicable for high-temperature and high mechanical load service conditions (e.g., aerospace or nuclear reactor components operating around 700–800°C) where thermal diffusion of interstitials is significant.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative details regarding the critical concentration of interstitials, the exact kinetics of precipitate nucleation/growth, and their spatial distribution remain uncertain and likely depend on specific alloy chemistry and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same HEA initially as a single-phase solid solution. One set (control) is processed and aged in an environment with minimal oxygen/nitrogen contamination (using high purity inert atmospheres), while the other set is intentionally aged in an oxygen/nitrogen-rich atmosphere under identical thermal and mechanical loading conditions. After aging, both sets are subjected to the same mechanical tests (e.g., tensile tests and fracture toughness measurements) and microstructural analyses (using TEM/SEM to detect precipitation).
measurements: Quantitative fracture toughness measurements and tensile ductility (e.g., elongation-to-failure).
High-resolution microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to detect and quantify nanoscale precipitates or secondary phases.
Chemical analysis (e.g., EDS, oxygen/nitrogen content measurements) to assess impurity segregation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen/nitrogen-rich aged samples do not exhibit any significant precipitate formation and there is no measurable decrease in toughness (i.e., similar mechanical performance and microstructure as the impurity-free control), then the hypothesis that impurity-induced precipitation is responsible for toughness loss and brittle fracture would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. In addition, some recent studies have highlighted the substantial impact of oxygen and nitrogen additions, in the range of 1 to 3 atomic % (at %) (, , ), on the mechanical properties of HEAs. For instance, Cui et al. () demonstrated that a Ti-V-Hf-Nb alloy with ~2 at % oxygen additions can reach a yield strength of 1.5 GPa, while maintaining substantial ductility. Similarly, Lei et al. () reported that by introducing 2 at % N, the tensile strength of a Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb alloy can surge by over 70%. These interstitials are often incorporated at trace levels during processing RHEAs and can accumulate further in service. However, a notable knowledge gap remains, especially regarding the behavior of these oxygen/nitrogen interstitials during high-temperature aging. In the present investigation, Ti-V-Nb-Ta samples were subjected to thermal aging for various durations at 700°C. The microstructure and mechanical properties of Ti-V-Nb-Ta before and after thermal aging were revealed by a combination of state-of-the-art microstructural characterization and nanoindentation techniques. Results indicate that impurity interstitials at the trace levels within the solid solution encourage the formation of α-Ti precipitates in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy when aged at high temperature, which undermines the effects of interstitial solid solution strengthening and leads to softening.
